name: Degexit'an
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: dege1248 Degexit'an (Deg Xinag/Ingalik) is not in the catalog. The single title-sweep item, Leer 1976 'Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan' (ANLA CA965L1976b), was located via Glottolog ref 167470, downloaded from the ANLA online store (86-page scan), and scanned (typescript pp. 1-30, two copies; handwritten draft pp. 61-86 not scanned-able). It is a comparative-historical study of the origin of TONE in Athabaskan from Proto-Athabaskan vowel constriction/stem-final glottalization; Ingalik is mentioned only for consonant reflexes, light:heavy stem forms and a final voicing contrast, and the word 'stress' does not occur — irrelevant to Deg Xinag word stress (priority none). The best first-hand stress statement actually read is Hargus 2010 (author PDF p. 7, fn. 12): 'Stress generally occurs on the final syllable in Deg Xinag polysyllables ending in a consonant (see Hargus 2005)', supported by root-stressed/prefix-unstressed statements in Hargus, Levow & Wright 2019 §7 and the Hargus 2008 handout. The authoritative source, Hargus 2005 'Stress in polysyllabic morphemes: Sekani and Deg Xinag' (ANLC Working Papers 5: 39-66), remains unobtained (no DOI; not on the author's site, ANLA, archive.org or ERIC) — high priority for print acquisition. Only the quotation-mark glyphs differ (typographic in the PDF). The reference list (PDF text lines 2081-2083) confirms Hargus 2005 = "Stress in polysyllabic morphemes: Sekani and Deg Xinag", Proceedings o…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In consonant-final polysyllabic words stress generally falls on the final syllable (Hargus 2010, fn. 12). In Deg Xinag, as in Athabaskan generally, that final closed syllable is the stem/root: Hargus, Levow & Wright 2019 (p. 41) state that root-initial consonants are 'consistently stressed' while prefix-initial ones are 'not stressed', and the 2012 slides mark stress on stems (təˈva, jənˈtətθ) and on suffix-less monosyllabic stems. So the working rule is: stress the root/stem syllable, which is word-final when the word ends in a consonant; the primary treatment (Hargus 2005, on stress inside polysyllabic morphemes) was not obtained, and vowel-final polysyllables are not covered by the quoted statement. A weight-sensitive reading (stress the closed final syllable) is the alternative literal reading of the quote.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'generally'; the statement is restricted to polysyllables ending in a consonant. Krauss 1962 notes 'long-heavy' stems (with a reconstructed suffix -e) and possible tone-glides, and that the dialect 'has not yet been definitively tonemicized'; Deg Xinag is treated as toneless by Hargus (2019 slides).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (polysyllabic words incl. verb prefix+stem complexes; citation forms in elicited word lists of the Yukon dialect). Krauss 1961 notes Chapman's and Osgood's transcriptions carried 'stress' marks that he omitted.
new_statements.identity_note: All Hargus data are from the Yukon dialect of Deg Xinag (Anvik, Shageluk, Holy Cross, Grayling); the Kuskokwim dialect (Stony River) is not covered by the stress statement. Glottolog dege1248 is the language-level code with no dialect subdivisions listed in the target record. Older names: Ingalik, Ten'a (Chapman), Deg Hit'an (Krauss 1974).

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the principal fieldworker on Yukon Deg Xinag: word stress is generally on the final syllable of consonant-final polysyllabic words (i.e., on the stem/root, since Athabaskan words are prefix + root; prefixes are unstressed per Hargus, Levow & Wright 2019 §7 and Hargus 2008 handout). It is a footnote-level summary that defers to Hargus 2005 (ANLC WP 5: 39-66, not obtained) for the full account; the qualifier 'generally' and the restriction to consonant-final polysyllables mean the vowel-final case is not stated here.

sources.quote: There are several suffixes which could result in giving rise to light:heavy stem pairs: the possessive suffix *-ə', the non-perfective negative suffix *-ə, and the verb nominalizing suffix *-(y)i' ... In Ingalik heavy stem forms have arisen both from the possessive suffix in nouns and the negative suffix in verbs. [typescript p. 23 = PDF p. 27] ... In some Koyukon and in Ingalik, suffixed ə is dropped following the voiced consonant, thus creating a surface contrast between the voiced and voiceless forms of these consonants in the positive and negative forms of verb stems. [typescript p. 18 = PDF p. 22]
sources.locator: Typescript pp. 1-30 (PDF pp. 2-30 and duplicate pp. 32-60); Ingalik mentioned at typescript p. 4 (retroflex series), p. 5 (*x reflex), p. 18 (PDF p. 22, final voiced:voiceless contrast), p. 23 (PDF p. 27, heavy stem forms), Chart of consonant reflexes (PDF p. 28)
sources.note: Nothing about word-stress placement in Ingalik/Deg Xinag. The paper is a comparative-historical account of how TONE (the 'suprasegmentals' of the title) arose in daughter languages from Proto-Athabaskan vowel constriction and stem-final glottalization (tone languages discussed: Navajo, Sarcee, Chipewyan, Kutchin, Carrier); Ingalik appears only for consonant reflexes, light:heavy stem forms and a final voicing contrast. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the scanned of the typescript.
